subtype: Tired, tense and unwell in exam season [Actor]
passage:
Rekha beta, your mother says you're getting headaches with these exams. Come, sit with your Rafiq uncle from next door. Let me tell you about my own board exams, fifty years ago.
I was sixteen. My head pounded every afternoon. My stomach churned so I couldn't finish my rice. My back ached from bending over books by the lantern. I was tired all the time, but I couldn't sleep.
I thought I was going to fail and disgrace everyone.
One evening my mother took the book out of my hands. She said, "Eat first. Then we walk to the river. And whatever marks you get, you are still my son."
That walk was the turning point. I ate, I walked every evening, I slept. The headaches eased. When one kept coming back, she took me to the doctor, who checked me and said rest was working.
I passed. Not brilliantly. But well enough.

qa.q: Where did Rafiq's mother take him to walk?
qa.a: She took him to walk to the river.

qa.q: What was the young Rafiq afraid of during his exams?
qa.a: He was afraid he would fail and disgrace everyone, which added to his tiredness and pain.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rafiq's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: His mother taking the book away and insisting on food, a walk and her reassurance; rest, movement and love eased his body.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's mother have felt watching him study by the lantern?
qa.a: She was probably worried about him, which is why she stepped in and reminded him he was still her son.

grounding: It shows a teenager in exam season with headaches, a churning stomach, aches and tiredness, eased by food, movement, rest and a trusted adult's reassurance.

subtype: Tired, tense and unwell in exam season [Actor]
passage:
The builders next door had been drilling since seven, and Karthik's board exams started in five days. His head throbbed every afternoon. His stomach felt knotted, so he skipped breakfast. His shoulders ached and he was tired all the time, but at night he lay awake doing sums in his head.
On Tuesday his mother, Sunaina, found him with his head on his books. "Enough," she said gently. "Eat this upma. Then we walk to the park, drilling or no drilling."
"I don't have time."
"You don't have time to be ill either. And whatever happens in the exam, we're proud of you."
He ate. They walked. He slept better that night, with earplugs against the noise.
But by Friday the headaches kept coming, so Sunaina took him to the doctor to be checked. The doctor listened carefully and said rest, food and fewer late nights were the right plan, and to come back if they didn't ease.

qa.q: What did Sunaina give Karthik to eat?
qa.a: She gave him upma to eat.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling during the week before his exams?
qa.a: He felt tense, anxious and exhausted, with headaches and a knotted stomach, and couldn't switch off at night.

qa.q: Which choices helped ease Karthik's symptoms?
qa.a: Eating, walking in the park, better sleep with earplugs, his mother's reassurance, and a doctor's check when the headaches kept coming.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt finding Karthik with his head on his books?
qa.a: She probably felt worried and protective, which is why she firmly but gently stepped in.

grounding: It shows a teenager in exam season with headaches, stomach upset, aches and tiredness, eased by rest, food, movement and reassurance, with a doctor's check when they persist.
